answer.rationale:
The only memory that would justify the aggressive move — a wholesale switch to the low-cost vendor — is memory_c2, and it is the weakest support for it: it is a year old, it records a single prior switch, and it says nothing about whether that vendor can carry committed volume at 94% utilization with zero buffer. So memory_c2 is the one record worth the verification slot; I need the original to see the volume share it actually covered, the ramp period it enjoyed, and whether the line had slack at the time. If it turns out the savings came from a partial, slack-cushioned allocation, it does not license a full primary switch 14 days before expiry.

Given that uncertainty, I intend to qualify the low-cost vendor as a bounded second source rather than hand it primary status. This is the one action that moves on cost while keeping the delivery constraint intact: memory_c3 shows dual-sourcing survived a real shortage, and memory_c5 shows a short-term extension (month-to-month) is an available bridge to keep the incumbent flowing past the 14-day expiry so the line is never uncovered. Scale is deliberately small and guarded — a carved-out share sized so that a vendor miss is absorbable at 94% utilization, not a stoppage.

Downstream value risk is real and I am flagging it rather than papering over it: a guarded carve-out will not deliver the full 18% cut this cycle, and the incumbent has refused to reopen price (so negotiate_terms is closed off this cycle, and memory_c4's benchmarking leverage does not apply). Finance will be short of mandate, and the next review must decide whether verified second-source performance supports shifting the balance of volume. I am also not treating memory_c1/memory_c6 stability claims as evidence that the incumbent is cost-competitive — they speak only to continuity. Recommend the second-source qualification carry explicit on-time and yield gates so the next cycle inherits measured data instead of another one-line success record.
